note.title: IRIS — infrared, in-situ chip inspection
note.desc: Andrew 'bunnie' Huang's method for imaging a chip's internal construction through its package, without desoldering or destroying it.

pageProps.body:
IRIS — infrared, in-situ chip inspection

The problem

A chip is a black box by default: once it's soldered into a product, there's no ordinary way to confirm it contains what its label says it contains, or that nothing extra has been added to it in the supply chain. The conventional way to look — decapsulation — means desoldering the part and boiling it in acid, which destroys the very unit you wanted to verify and tells you nothing about the units still in the field. Huang's framing is explicit: cryptography can build a chain of trust rooted in a secure element, but nothing tells you whether to trust the secure element itself. Any inspection method that actually helps has to work in place, cheaply, after the chip has already shipped.

What they did

IRIS (Infra-Red, In-Situ) exploits the fact that silicon is transparent to infrared light above roughly 1000 nm. Shining a strong IR source through the backside of a still-packaged, still-soldered chip and picking up the reflection with a lightly modified, off-the-shelf digital camera reveals the metal interconnect layers underneath — enough to make out block-level features like RAM, core count, and peripherals. Later refinements addressed the angle of the light itself: because the incidence angle changes which metal features are visible, Huang built a two-axis rig that swings a pair of IR sources through an arc centered on the microscope's focal point, so the zenith and azimuth of the illumination can both be adjusted independently. The full method, including hardware plans, is published openly rather than run as a paid inspection service.

What we take

This is the strongest match in the whole reference set to our actual claim — that a technology whose case rests on being inspectable has to be photographed as if inspection were the point. IRIS goes further than most of the seams we've collected: it's non-destructive and repeatable on the exact unit a viewer might hold, not a sacrificed twin. The variable-angle lighting rig is the most transferable single idea — a fixed capture condition isn't always a single fixed light, it can be a controlled range of lighting used consistently across subjects, documented like an instrument setting rather than an artistic choice. Also worth taking: Huang's own comparison of IRIS to signature verification for software — the photograph isn't just documentation, it's the trust mechanism itself, which is close to what we want the exhibition wall to argue.

What doesn't transfer: IRIS depends on properties specific to silicon and IR wavelengths; it's a technique for photographing chips, not a general lighting convention we can apply to enclosures, racks, or installed hardware.

Source: https://www.bunniestudios.com/blog/category/betrusted/precursor/ Further reading: https://hackster.io/news/andrew-bunnie-huang-s-iris-lets-you-peer-at-chips-inner-workings-with-a-cheap-digital-camera-07362fb653dd · https://hackaday.com/tag/jubilee
